Name: Application Security Verification Standard Project
Description: The Application Security Verification Standard is a list of application security requirements that architects, developers, testers, security professionals, tool vendors, and consumers can use to define, build, test, and verify secure applications.

Assessment.Scope: All ASVS 5.0.0 Level 1 and Level 2 requirements. Level 3 requirements are included unchanged from the source document without assessment fields.

Legend.Applicability: yes = requirement applies to this project; no = out of scope (e.g. Immich is not an authorization server, no LDAP/SAML/WebRTC); partial = applies only in part or depends on deployment.
Legend.Implemented: yes = implemented; partial = partially implemented or delegated to deployment/reverse proxy; no = not implemented; n/a = not applicable.
Legend.Tested: yes = sufficient automated test coverage found; partial = some related tests exist but do not fully verify the requirement; no = no coverage found; n/a = not applicable.

Items.Description: Verify that input is decoded or unescaped into a canonical form only once, it is only decoded when encoded data in that form is expected, and that this is done before processing the input further, for example it is not performed after input validation or sanitization.
Items.Evidence: Neither the server nor the web layer performs additional decoding/unescaping of input: zod validates raw strings and NestJS does not auto-decode bodies, so no double-decode or post-validation decoding occurs.

Items.Description: Verify that the application performs output encoding and escaping either as a final step before being used by the interpreter for which it is intended or by the interpreter itself.
Items.Evidence: Output encoding happens at the last step: Svelte escapes at render time and NestJS serializes JSON at response time; no pre-encoded fragments are stored and re-emitted.

Items.Description: Verify that output encoding for an HTTP response, HTML document, or XML document is relevant for the context required, such as encoding the relevant characters for HTML elements, HTML attributes, HTML comments, CSS, or HTTP header fields, to avoid changing the message or document structure.
Items.Evidence: Web UI is Svelte, which context-escapes all interpolated output by default; API responses are serialized JSON (server/src/controllers, web/src). No manual HTML string building found.

Items.Description: Verify that when dynamically building URLs, untrusted data is encoded according to its context (e.g., URL encoding or base64url encoding for query or path parameters). Ensure that only safe URL protocols are permitted (e.g., disallow javascript: or data:).
Items.Evidence: Web builds URLs from route params and API responses; no explicit URL-encoding validation or javascript:/data: protocol allowlist was found in dynamic URL construction.

Items.Description: Verify that output encoding or escaping is used when dynamically building JavaScript content (including JSON), to avoid changing the message or document structure (to avoid JavaScript and JSON injection).
Items.Evidence: All API responses are JSON serialized by NestJS; the web app consumes JSON via typed fetch wrappers and renders through Svelte's escaping. No dynamic JS/JSON string building found.

Items.Description: Verify that data selection or database queries (e.g., SQL, HQL, NoSQL, Cypher) use parameterized queries, ORMs, entity frameworks, or are otherwise protected from SQL Injection and other database injection attacks. This is also relevant when writing stored procedures.
Items.Evidence: Server uses Kysely query builder with bound parameters (server/src/repositories); the few sql.raw/sql fragments interpolate only internal constants (e.g. interval strings, array casts), not user input.

Items.Description: Verify that the application protects against OS command injection and that operating system calls use parameterized OS queries or use contextual command line output encoding.
Items.Evidence: External tools (ffmpeg, exiftool) are invoked via child_process spawn with argument arrays and no shell interpolation (server/src/repositories/process.repository.ts); user data never reaches a shell command line.

Items.Description: Verify that the application protects against LDAP injection vulnerabilities, or that specific security controls to prevent LDAP injection have been implemented.
Items.Evidence: The application has no LDAP integration; the only directory-style data is its own Postgres user table.

Items.Description: Verify that the application is protected against XPath injection attacks by using query parameterization or precompiled queries.
Items.Evidence: No XPath queries are used anywhere in server or machine-learning code.

Items.Description: Verify that LaTeX processors are configured securely (such as not using the "--shell-escape" flag) and an allowlist of commands is used to prevent LaTeX injection attacks.
Items.Evidence: No LaTeX processing exists in the project.

Items.Description: Verify that the application escapes special characters in regular expressions (typically using a backslash) to prevent them from being misinterpreted as metacharacters.
Items.Evidence: The one dynamic-regex site escapes special characters before building the pattern (server/src/utils/workflow.ts isAllowedHost escapes regex metacharacters around '*' wildcards); no other RegExp is built from user input. Covered by workflow utils spec.

Items.Description: Verify that the application is protected against CSV and Formula Injection. The application must follow the escaping rules defined in RFC 4180 sections 2.6 and 2.7 when exporting CSV content. Additionally, when exporting to CSV or other spreadsheet formats (such as XLS, XLSX, or ODF), special characters (including '=', '+', '-', '@', '\t' (tab), and '\0' (null character)) must be escaped with a single quote if they appear as the first character in a field value.
Verify that all untrusted HTML input from WYSIWYG editors or similar is sanitized using a well-known and secure HTML sanitization library or framework feature.
Items.Evidence: Immich accepts no HTML input: there is no WYSIWYG editor; all user text (descriptions, names, comments) is stored and rendered as escaped text by Svelte.

Items.Description: Verify that the application avoids the use of eval() or other dynamic code execution features such as Spring Expression Language (SpEL). Where there is no alternative, any user input being included must be sanitized before being executed.
Items.Evidence: No eval()/new Function() in server or web source. External plugins execute in a separate sandboxed process and are admin-installed packages, not user input.

Items.Description: Verify that data being passed to a potentially dangerous context is sanitized beforehand to enforce safety measures, such as only allowing characters which are safe for this context and trimming input which is too long.
Items.Evidence: Filenames are sanitized before storage (sanitize() in asset-media.service.ts) and zod enforces lengths/formats on most inputs, but there is no general 'safe character set' policy for all free-text fields.

Items.Description: Verify that user-supplied Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) scriptable content is validated or sanitized to contain only tags and attributes (such as draw graphics) that are safe for the application, e.g., do not contain scripts and foreignObject.
Items.Evidence: .svg is accepted as an asset and profile image (server/src/utils/mime-types.ts) and served inline with its real content type; SVG content is never sanitized. Mitigated by the helmet CSP (script-src 'self') on API responses and by images being rendered via in the UI, but direct navigation to an SVG original is not blocked.

Items.Description: Verify that the application sanitizes or disables user-supplied scriptable or expression template language content, such as Markdown, CSS or XSL stylesheets, BBCode, or similar.
Items.Evidence: Users cannot supply Markdown, CSS, XSL or BBCode that is later rendered; all user text is plain text.

Items.Description: Verify that the application protects against Server-side Request Forgery (SSRF) attacks, by validating untrusted data against an allowlist of protocols, domains, paths and ports and sanitizing potentially dangerous characters before using the data to call another service.
Items.Evidence: All outbound HTTP targets (version check, ML service, OAuth issuer/JWKS, map/reverse-geocode endpoints) are fixed constants or admin-configured settings, not end-user input; there is no URL allowlist validation of admin-entered URLs beyond new URL() parsing.

Items.Description: Verify that the application protects against template injection attacks by not allowing templates to be built based on untrusted input. Where there is no alternative, any untrusted input being included dynamically during template creation must be sanitized or strictly validated.
Items.Evidence: Emails are rendered from fixed React-email templates with bound props (server/src/emails); no template strings are composed from user input.

Items.Description: Verify that the application appropriately sanitizes untrusted input before use in Java Naming and Directory Interface (JNDI) queries and that JNDI is configured securely to prevent JNDI injection attacks.
Items.Evidence: No Java/JNDI anywhere in the stack (Node.js server, Python ML, Rust native modules).

Items.Description: Verify that the application sanitizes content before it is sent to memcache to prevent injection attacks.
Items.Evidence: Redis is accessed exclusively through ioredis (binary-safe RESP protocol) with structured arguments; no memcached-style text commands are concatenated with user input.

Items.Description: Verify that format strings which might resolve in an unexpected or malicious way when used are sanitized before being processed.
Items.Evidence: No printf-style format APIs are used with user input; all string formatting is JavaScript template literals, which are not format-string vulnerable.

Items.Description: Verify that the application sanitizes user input before passing to mail systems to protect against SMTP or IMAP injection.
Items.Evidence: Email sending uses nodemailer with structured message objects; recipient addresses are validated by zod (toEmail) before use, preventing header injection.

Items.Description: Verify that regular expressions are free from elements causing exponential backtracking, and ensure untrusted input is sanitized to mitigate ReDoS or Runaway Regex attacks.
Verify that the application uses memory-safe string, safer memory copy and pointer arithmetic to detect or prevent stack, buffer, or heap overflows.
Items.Evidence: The server is TypeScript/Node (memory-safe runtime) and native components are Rust; no manual pointer arithmetic or unsafe string copies exist in JS/TS code. Rust/native code is not memory-audited here.

Items.Description: Verify that sign, range, and input validation techniques are used to prevent integer overflows.
Items.Evidence: JavaScript numbers are 64-bit and zod enforces ranges on many fields (e.g. lat/lon bounds, counts); no explicit integer-overflow checks exist for size counters used in upload accounting.

Items.Description: Verify that dynamically allocated memory and resources are released, and that references or pointers to freed memory are removed or set to null to prevent dangling pointers and use-after-free vulnerabilities.
Items.Evidence: Streams are piped with error handlers and cleaned up on failure (file-upload.interceptor.ts), DB connections are pooled by Kysely, and child processes are awaited/errored; no manual free() patterns exist in a GC runtime.

Items.Description: Verify that the application configures XML parsers to use a restrictive configuration and that unsafe features such as resolving external entities are disabled to prevent XML eXternal Entity (XXE) attacks.
Items.Evidence: XMP sidecar uploads are parsed with exiftool as an external tool (server/src/services/metadata.service.ts); no in-process XML parser with external-entity resolution is used in server or ML code.

Items.Description: Verify that deserialization of untrusted data enforces safe input handling, such as using an allowlist of object types or restricting client-defined object types, to prevent deserialization attacks. Deserialization mechanisms that are explicitly defined as insecure must not be used with untrusted input.
Items.Evidence: Only JSON.parse of request bodies (via zod validation) is performed; no object-type-directed deserialization (no unserialize, no class-transformer of untrusted payloads) exists.

Items.Description: Verify that different parsers used in the application for the same data type (e.g., JSON parsers, XML parsers, URL parsers), perform parsing in a consistent way and use the same character encoding mechanism to avoid issues such as JSON Interoperability vulnerabilities or different URI or file parsing behavior being exploited in Remote File Inclusion (RFI) or Server-side Request Forgery (SSRF) attacks.

Verify that the application's documentation defines input validation rules for how to check the validity of data items against an expected structure. This could be common data formats such as credit card numbers, email addresses, telephone numbers, or it could be an internal data format.
Items.Evidence: DTO schemas are defined with zod and annotated with descriptions/examples, exposed via generated OpenAPI spec (server/src/dtos, open-api). This documents expected structures, but there is no dedicated input-validation documentation.

Items.Description: Verify that the application's documentation defines how to validate the logical and contextual consistency of combined data items, such as checking that suburb and ZIP code match.
Items.Evidence: No documentation defines cross-field consistency rules for combined data items.

Items.Description: Verify that expectations for business logic limits and validations are documented, including both per-user and globally across the application.
Items.Evidence: Global business limits exist in code (storage quotas per user, job concurrency), and quotas are documented in the admin UI, but there is no consolidated documentation of business-logic limits.

Items.Description: Verify that input is validated to enforce business or functional expectations for that input. This should either use positive validation against an allow list of values, patterns, and ranges, or be based on comparing the input to an expected structure and logical limits according to predefined rules. For L1, this can focus on input which is used to make specific business or security decisions. For L2 and up, this should apply to all input.
Items.Evidence: Every endpoint DTO is validated by zod schemas (server/src/dtos, validation.ts) with typed constraints (lengths, enums, UUIDs, regex); server/test/validation.spec.ts covers parts of the schema surface.

Items.Description: Verify that the application is designed to enforce input validation at a trusted service layer. While client-side validation improves usability and should be encouraged, it must not be relied upon as a security control.
Items.Evidence: Validation runs in the NestJS server via zod DTOs; web/mobile validation is UX-only. The security-relevant decisions (auth, permissions, quotas) are all validated server-side.

Items.Description: Verify that the application ensures that combinations of related data items are reasonable according to the pre-defined rules.
Items.Evidence: Some combined-field rules are enforced (e.g. shared-link expiry after creation, album user permissions), but there is no systematic cross-field consistency validation across all DTOs.

Items.Description: Verify that the application will only process business logic flows for the same user in the expected sequential step order and without skipping steps.
Items.Evidence: Critical flows are sequence-guarded: admin onboarding is only available before an admin exists (auth.guard.ts setup routes) and setup is disabled afterwards; most other flows are single-step and need no ordering.

Items.Description: Verify that business logic limits are implemented per the application's documentation to avoid business logic flaws being exploited.
Items.Evidence: Quotas are enforced at upload time and job concurrency is bounded, but these limits are not derived from documented expectations; some flows lack explicit business limits.

Items.Description: Verify that transactions are being used at the business logic level such that either a business logic operation succeeds in its entirety or it is rolled back to the previous correct state.
Items.Evidence: Multi-step operations run inside database transactions (Kysely transaction(), e.g. asset deletion, trash restore); covered partially by repository/service specs.

Items.Description: Verify that business logic level locking mechanisms are used to ensure that limited quantity resources (such as theater seats or delivery slots) cannot be double-booked by manipulating the application's logic.
Items.Evidence: The domain has no limited-quantity resources to double-book; DB unique constraints (e.g. asset checksum per owner, session tokens) prevent duplicate creation instead.

Items.Description: Verify that high-value business logic flows require multi-user approval to prevent unauthorized or accidental actions. This could include but is not limited to large monetary transfers, contract approvals, access to classified information, or safety overrides in manufacturing.

Verify that anti-automation controls are in place to protect against excessive calls to application functions that could lead to data exfiltration, garbage-data creation, quota exhaustion, rate-limit breaches, denial-of-service, or overuse of costly resources.
Items.Evidence: No anti-automation controls exist for any endpoint (no throttling, per-user API quotas, or costly-resource limits beyond job queue concurrency).

Items.Description: Verify that business logic flows require realistic human timing, preventing excessively rapid transaction submissions.

Verify that application documentation states the expected security features that browsers using the application must support (such as HTTPS, HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS), Content Security Policy (CSP), and other relevant HTTP security mechanisms). It must also define how the application must behave when some of these features are not available (such as warning the user or blocking access).

Verify that security controls are in place to prevent browsers from rendering content or functionality in HTTP responses in an incorrect context (e.g., when an API, a user-uploaded file or other resource is requested directly). Possible controls could include: not serving the content unless HTTP request header fields (such as Sec-Fetch-\*) indicate it is the correct context, using the sandbox directive of the Content-Security-Policy header field or using the attachment disposition type in the Content-Disposition header field.
Items.Evidence: User-uploaded files are never served from a public folder; they are streamed through authenticated API routes with explicit Content-Type (server/src/controllers/assets). No CSP sandbox or Content-Disposition: attachment hardening for inline rendering contexts.

Items.Description: Verify that content intended to be displayed as text, rather than rendered as HTML, is handled using safe rendering functions (such as createTextNode or textContent) to prevent unintended execution of content such as HTML or JavaScript.
Items.Evidence: The web app renders untrusted content (file names, comments, metadata) exclusively through Svelte text interpolation, which escapes by default; no innerHTML/dangerouslySetInnerHTML usage found.

Items.Description: Verify that the application avoids DOM clobbering when using client-side JavaScript by employing explicit variable declarations, performing strict type checking, avoiding storing global variables on the document object, and implementing namespace isolation.
Verify that cookies have the 'Secure' attribute set, and if the '\__Host-' prefix is not used for the cookie name, the '__Secure-' prefix must be used for the cookie name.
Items.Evidence: Auth cookies are HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax and Secure when the connection is secure (server/src/utils/response.ts), but names (immich_access etc.) lack the __Host-/__Secure- prefix and the Secure flag depends on request protocol. Cookie attributes asserted in server/src/controllers/auth.controller.spec.ts.

Items.Description: Verify that each cookie's 'SameSite' attribute value is set according to the purpose of the cookie, to limit exposure to user interface redress attacks and browser-based request forgery attacks, commonly known as cross-site request forgery (CSRF).
Items.Evidence: All cookies use SameSite=Lax (server/src/utils/response.ts), which suits the session/CSRF purpose, but no cookie gets a purpose-specific decision (e.g. Strict for auth) and the non-HttpOnly isAuthenticated cookie signals auth state.

Items.Description: Verify that cookies have the '__Host-' prefix for the cookie name unless they are explicitly designed to be shared with other hosts.
Items.Evidence: No cookie uses the __Host- prefix (immich_access, immich_is_authenticated, etc.); they are served on the same host across API and web paths.

Items.Description: Verify that if the value of a cookie is not meant to be accessible to client-side scripts (such as a session token), the cookie must have the 'HttpOnly' attribute set and the same value (e. g. session token) must only be transferred to the client via the 'Set-Cookie' header field.
Items.Evidence: The access-token cookie is HttpOnly and set via Set-Cookie, but the same session token is also returned in the login response body (mapLoginResponse) for mobile/API clients, violating the Set-Cookie-only rule. Cookie attributes asserted in auth.controller.spec.ts.

Items.Description: Verify that when the application writes a cookie, the cookie name and value length combined are not over 4096 bytes. Overly large cookies will not be stored by the browser and therefore not sent with requests, preventing the user from using application functionality which relies on that cookie.

Verify that a Strict-Transport-Security header field is included on all responses to enforce an HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) policy. A maximum age of at least 1 year must be defined, and for L2 and up, the policy must apply to all subdomains as well.
Items.Evidence: Helmet middleware is enabled in production (server/src/app.common.ts), which sends HSTS by default, but with helmet's default max-age of 180 days (< 1 year) and without includeSubDomains; no explicit HSTS configuration.

Items.Description: Verify that the Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) Access-Control-Allow-Origin header field is a fixed value by the application, or if the Origin HTTP request header field value is used, it is validated against an allowlist of trusted origins. When 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *' needs to be used, verify that the response does not include any sensitive information.
Items.Evidence: CORS is only enabled in development (app.enableCors() guarded by isDev()); production responses send no Access-Control-Allow-Origin at all, so cross-origin browser access is blocked rather than reflected.

Items.Description: Verify that HTTP responses include a Content-Security-Policy response header field which defines directives to ensure the browser only loads and executes trusted content or resources, in order to limit execution of malicious JavaScript. As a minimum, a global policy must be used which includes the directives object-src 'none' and base-uri 'none' and defines either an allowlist or uses nonces or hashes. For an L3 application, a per-response policy with nonces or hashes must be defined.
Items.Evidence: A global CSP is configured via helmet.json with object-src 'none' and script-src 'self', but base-uri is 'self' instead of 'none' and no nonces/hashes are used for scripts (hashes are auto-applied only to style directives via applyCspHashes).

Items.Description: Verify that all HTTP responses contain an 'X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff' header field. This instructs browsers not to use content sniffing and MIME type guessing for the given response, and to require the response's Content-Type header field value to match the destination resource. For example, the response to a request for a style is only accepted if the response's Content-Type is 'text/css'. This also enables the use of the Cross-Origin Read Blocking (CORB) functionality by the browser.
Items.Evidence: Helmet defaults include X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff on all responses (helmet middleware applied in app.common.ts before routes); no test asserts the header.

Items.Description: Verify that the application sets a referrer policy to prevent leakage of technically sensitive data to third-party services via the 'Referer' HTTP request header field. This can be done using the Referrer-Policy HTTP response header field or via HTML element attributes. Sensitive data could include path and query data in the URL, and for internal non-public applications also the hostname.
Items.Evidence: Helmet defaults set a Referrer-Policy header (no-referrer) on all responses; no test asserts the header.

Items.Description: Verify that the web application uses the frame-ancestors directive of the Content-Security-Policy header field for every HTTP response to ensure that it cannot be embedded by default and that embedding of specific resources is allowed only when necessary. Note that the X-Frame-Options header field, although supported by browsers, is obsolete and may not be relied upon.
Items.Evidence: The CSP in helmet.json has no frame-ancestors directive; only helmet's default X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN (frameguard) protects against embedding, which the requirement considers obsolete.

Items.Description: Verify that the Content-Security-Policy header field specifies a location to report violations.

Verify that all HTTP responses that initiate a document rendering (such as responses with Content-Type text/html), include the Cross‑Origin‑Opener‑Policy header field with the same-origin directive or the same-origin-allow-popups directive as required. This prevents attacks that abuse shared access to Window objects, such as tabnabbing and frame counting.

Verify that, if the application does not rely on the CORS preflight mechanism to prevent disallowed cross-origin requests to use sensitive functionality, these requests are validated to ensure they originate from the application itself. This may be done by using and validating anti-forgery tokens or requiring extra HTTP header fields that are not CORS-safelisted request-header fields. This is to defend against browser-based request forgery attacks, commonly known as cross-site request forgery (CSRF).
Items.Evidence: No anti-forgery tokens. CSRF defense relies on SameSite=Lax cookies plus the absence of CORS headers in production; cookie attributes and auth flow are covered by auth.controller.spec.ts and e2e/src/specs/web/auth.e2e-spec.ts.

Items.Description: Verify that, if the application relies on the CORS preflight mechanism to prevent disallowed cross-origin use of sensitive functionality, it is not possible to call the functionality with a request which does not trigger a CORS-preflight request. This may require checking the values of the 'Origin' and 'Content-Type' request header fields or using an extra header field that is not a CORS-safelisted header-field.
Items.Evidence: The app does not rely on CORS preflight; state-changing endpoints expect JSON bodies (non-safelisted content type) and cookies are SameSite=Lax, so cross-site requests carry no credentials for POSTs. No explicit Origin/Content-Type validation tests.

Items.Description: Verify that HTTP requests to sensitive functionality use appropriate HTTP methods such as POST, PUT, PATCH, or DELETE, and not methods defined by the HTTP specification as "safe" such as HEAD, OPTIONS, or GET. Alternatively, strict validation of the Sec-Fetch-* request header fields can be used to ensure that the request did not originate from an inappropriate cross-origin call, a navigation request, or a resource load (such as an image source) where this is not expected.
Items.Evidence: All state-changing API routes use POST/PUT/DELETE/PATCH via NestJS controllers; GET routes are read-only. No explicit test asserts method usage per route.

Items.Description: Verify that separate applications are hosted on different hostnames to leverage the restrictions provided by same-origin policy, including how documents or scripts loaded by one origin can interact with resources from another origin and hostname-based restrictions on cookies.
Items.Evidence: Immich is a single application serving web and API from one origin; there are no separate applications to isolate on different hostnames.

Items.Description: Verify that messages received by the postMessage interface are discarded if the origin of the message is not trusted, or if the syntax of the message is invalid.
Items.Evidence: postMessage is used only for Web Workers (hash-file, file-uploader) and service-worker messaging (web/src/lib/utils/sw-messenger.ts), which are same-origin by construction; no listener accepts cross-origin messages.

Items.Description: Verify that JSONP functionality is not enabled anywhere across the application to avoid Cross-Site Script Inclusion (XSSI) attacks.
Verify that data requiring authorization is not included in script resource responses, like JavaScript files, to prevent Cross-Site Script Inclusion (XSSI) attacks.

Verify that authenticated resources (such as images, videos, scripts, and other documents) can be loaded or embedded on behalf of the user only when intended. This can be accomplished by strict validation of the Sec-Fetch-* HTTP request header fields to ensure that the request did not originate from an inappropriate cross-origin call, or by setting a restrictive Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy HTTP response header field to instruct the browser to block returned content.

Verify that client-side assets, such as JavaScript libraries, CSS, or web fonts, are only hosted externally (e.g., on a Content Delivery Network) if the resource is static and versioned and Subresource Integrity (SRI) is used to validate the integrity of the asset. If this is not possible, there should be a documented security decision to justify this for each resource.

Verify that the application only uses client-side technologies which are still supported and considered secure. Examples of technologies which do not meet this requirement include NSAPI plugins, Flash, Shockwave, ActiveX, Silverlight, NACL, or client-side Java applets.
Items.Evidence: Client-side stack is Svelte (web) and Flutter (mobile); no Flash/ActiveX/Silverlight/applet or other unsupported plugin technology is used.

Items.Description: Verify that the application will only automatically redirect the user to a different hostname or domain (which is not controlled by the application) where the destination appears on an allowlist.
Items.Evidence: Redirects to other hosts occur only in the OAuth flow (to the configured IdP and back via the configured redirect URI, incl. mobile redirect handling) and to the IdP logout endpoint; these are admin-configured, effectively an allowlist. No generic redirect parameters were found.

Items.Description: Verify that the application shows a notification when the user is being redirected to a URL outside of the application's control, with an option to cancel the navigation.

Verify that the application's top-level domain (e.g., site.tld) is added to the public preload list for HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS). This ensures that the use of TLS for the application is built directly into the main browsers, rather than relying only on the Strict-Transport-Security response header field.
Verify that the application behaves as documented (such as warning the user or blocking access) if the browser used to access the application does not support the expected security features.

Verify that every HTTP response with a message body contains a Content-Type header field that matches the actual content of the response, including the charset parameter to specify safe character encoding (e.g., UTF-8, ISO-8859-1) according to IANA Media Types, such as "text/", "/+xml" and "/xml".
Items.Evidence: NestJS/Express sets application/json; charset=utf-8 for API responses; asset/file responses set the correct media type from the internal mime-type map. Covered indirectly by API e2e specs.

Items.Description: Verify that only user-facing endpoints (intended for manual web-browser access) automatically redirect from HTTP to HTTPS, while other services or endpoints do not implement transparent redirects. This is to avoid a situation where a client is erroneously sending unencrypted HTTP requests, but since the requests are being automatically redirected to HTTPS, the leakage of sensitive data goes undiscovered.
Items.Evidence: The app never issues HTTP->HTTPS redirects itself; this is a reverse-proxy concern. The API endpoints respond directly without redirects, satisfying the 'no transparent redirects for non-browser clients' intent at the app layer.

Items.Description: Verify that any HTTP header field used by the application and set by an intermediary layer, such as a load balancer, a web proxy, or a backend-for-frontend service, cannot be overridden by the end-user. Example headers might include X-Real-IP, X-Forwarded-*, or X-User-ID.
Items.Evidence: Express is configured with 'trust proxy' limited to loopback + admin-configured trustedProxies (app.common.ts), so X-Forwarded-* from untrusted hops are ignored and clientIp comes from a trusted field. Covered partially by auth.service.spec.ts IP handling.

Items.Description: Verify that only HTTP methods that are explicitly supported by the application or its API (including OPTIONS during preflight requests) can be used and that unused methods are blocked.

Verify that per-message digital signatures are used to provide additional assurance on top of transport protections for requests or transactions which are highly sensitive or which traverse a number of systems.

Verify that all application components (including load balancers, firewalls, and application servers) determine boundaries of incoming HTTP messages using the appropriate mechanism for the HTTP version to prevent HTTP request smuggling. In HTTP/1.x, if a Transfer-Encoding header field is present, the Content-Length header must be ignored per RFC 2616. When using HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, if a Content-Length header field is present, the receiver must ensure that it is consistent with the length of the DATA frames.
Items.Evidence: HTTP message framing is handled by Node's HTTP server and Express per RFC; no custom framing/parsing code exists. Intermediary behavior is a deployment concern.

Items.Description: Verify that when generating HTTP messages, the Content-Length header field does not conflict with the length of the content as determined by the framing of the HTTP protocol, in order to prevent request smuggling attacks.

Verify that the application does not send nor accept HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 messages with connection-specific header fields such as Transfer-Encoding to prevent response splitting and header injection attacks.

Verify that the application only accepts HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 requests where the header fields and values do not contain any CR (\r), LF (\n), or CRLF (\r\n) sequences, to prevent header injection attacks.

Verify that, if the application (backend or frontend) builds and sends requests, it uses validation, sanitization, or other mechanisms to avoid creating URIs (such as for API calls) or HTTP request header fields (such as Authorization or Cookie), which are too long to be accepted by the receiving component. This could cause a denial of service, such as when sending an overly long request (e.g., a long cookie header field), which results in the server always responding with an error status.

Verify that a query allowlist, depth limiting, amount limiting, or query cost analysis is used to prevent GraphQL or data layer expression Denial of Service (DoS) as a result of expensive, nested queries.
Items.Evidence: The API is REST/JSON; no GraphQL endpoint exists.

Items.Description: Verify that GraphQL introspection queries are disabled in the production environment unless the GraphQL API is meant to be used by other parties.
Items.Evidence: No GraphQL API exists.

Items.Description: Verify that WebSocket over TLS (WSS) is used for all WebSocket connections.
Items.Evidence: WebSockets are served on the same HTTP server as the API (server/src/middleware/websocket.adapter.ts); TLS is terminated by the reverse proxy, the app itself listens on plain HTTP inside the container network.

Items.Description: Verify that, during the initial HTTP WebSocket handshake, the Origin header field is checked against a list of origins allowed for the application.
Items.Evidence: The socket.io server (websocket.adapter.ts) sets no Origin allowlist; connections are authenticated by session cookie but the handshake Origin is not validated.

Items.Description: Verify that, if the application's standard session management cannot be used, dedicated tokens are being used for this, which comply with the relevant Session Management security requirements.
Items.Evidence: WebSocket channels reuse the standard session management (same cookies/session tokens as HTTP) rather than a separate weaker mechanism; the web client passes the access token during the socket handshake.

Items.Description: Verify that dedicated WebSocket session management tokens are initially obtained or validated through the previously authenticated HTTPS session when transitioning an existing HTTPS session to a WebSocket channel.
Items.Evidence: The WS session is established from the already-authenticated HTTPS session (cookie/handshake token validated against the session table); no unauthenticated WS transition exists. Covered partially by e2e/src/specs/web/websocket.e2e-spec.ts.

Items.Description: Verify that the documentation defines the permitted file types, expected file extensions, and maximum size (including unpacked size) for each upload feature. Additionally, ensure that the documentation specifies how files are made safe for end-users to download and process, such as how the application behaves when a malicious file is detected.
Items.Evidence: docs describe supported media formats at a high level and the admin UI shows quota settings, but there is no documentation of per-upload maximum sizes or malicious-file handling behavior.

Items.Description: Verify that the application will only accept files of a size which it can process without causing a loss of performance or a denial of service attack.
Items.Evidence: Multer is configured without file size limits (server/src/middleware/file-upload.interceptor.ts) and the JSON body limit (10mb) does not apply to multipart uploads; no server-side upload size cap exists, relying on reverse proxy limits.

Items.Description: Verify that when the application accepts a file, either on its own or within an archive such as a zip file, it checks if the file extension matches an expected file extension and validates that the contents correspond to the type represented by the extension. This includes, but is not limited to, checking the initial 'magic bytes', performing image re-writing, and using specialized libraries for file content validation. For L1, this can focus just on files which are used to make specific business or security decisions. For L2 and up, this must apply to all files being accepted.
Items.Evidence: Upload fileFilter allowlists extensions per upload type (asset/sidecar/profile via mimeTypes.isAsset etc.); actual content is validated later by ffprobe/exiftool processing and thumbnail generation, not by magic bytes at upload time. Covered partially by e2e/src/specs/server/api/asset.e2e-spec.ts.

Items.Description: Verify that the application checks compressed files (e.g., zip, gz, docx, odt) against maximum allowed uncompressed size and against maximum number of files before uncompressing the file.
Items.Evidence: No archive formats (zip, gz, docx) are accepted as uploads; only media files, XMP sidecars and profile images pass the extension allowlist.

Items.Description: Verify that a file size quota and maximum number of files per user are enforced to ensure that a single user cannot fill up the storage with too many files, or excessively large files.

Verify that the application does not allow uploading compressed files containing symlinks unless this is specifically required (in which case it will be necessary to enforce an allowlist of the files that can be symlinked to).
Verify that the application rejects uploaded images with a pixel size larger than the maximum allowed, to prevent pixel flood attacks.
Verify that files uploaded or generated by untrusted input and stored in a public folder, are not executed as server-side program code when accessed directly with an HTTP request.
Items.Evidence: Uploads are stored in a storage folder outside the web root and served only through authenticated API endpoints that stream the file with a safe Content-Type; the static web root contains only built assets.

Items.Description: Verify that when the application creates file paths for file operations, instead of user-submitted filenames, it uses internally generated or trusted data, or if user-submitted filenames or file metadata must be used, strict validation and sanitization must be applied. This is to protect against path traversal, local or remote file inclusion (LFI, RFI), and server-side request forgery (SSRF) attacks.
Items.Evidence: Stored filenames are generated server-side: uuid + sanitized extension (asset-media.service.ts getUploadFilename uses sanitize() and only takes the extension from user input); folders are built from internal ids/uuids, preventing traversal.

Items.Description: Verify that server-side file processing, such as file decompression, ignores user-provided path information to prevent vulnerabilities such as zip slip.

Verify that the application validates or ignores user-submitted filenames, including in a JSON, JSONP, or URL parameter and specifies a filename in the Content-Disposition header field in the response.
Items.Evidence: Download responses set Content-Disposition with RFC 5987/6266 encoding (server/src/utils/file.ts filename*=UTF-8''..., integrity-admin.controller.ts uses attachment + encodeURIComponent); stored filenames are server-generated, user filenames are only echoed in this encoded form.

Items.Description: Verify that file names served (e.g., in HTTP response header fields or email attachments) are encoded or sanitized (e.g., following RFC 6266) to preserve document structure and prevent injection attacks.
Items.Evidence: Filenames in Content-Disposition are RFC 5987 encoded (filename*=UTF-8'' + encodeURIComponent), preventing header injection and preserving structure.

Items.Description: Verify that files obtained from untrusted sources are scanned by antivirus scanners to prevent serving of known malicious content.
Items.Evidence: No antivirus scanning of uploaded files exists; content is processed by ffmpeg/exiftool/sharp but not scanned for malware.

Items.Description: Verify that application documentation defines how controls such as rate limiting, anti-automation, and adaptive response, are used to defend against attacks such as credential stuffing and password brute force. The documentation must make clear how these controls are configured and prevent malicious account lockout.
Items.Evidence: No documentation defines rate limiting, anti-automation or adaptive response controls for login; docs only mention reverse proxy setup in general.

Items.Description: Verify that a list of context-specific words is documented in order to prevent their use in passwords. The list could include permutations of organization names, product names, system identifiers, project codenames, department or role names, and similar.
Items.Evidence: No context-specific word list (organization/product names) is documented for password screening.

Items.Description: Verify that, if the application includes multiple authentication pathways, these are all documented together with the security controls and authentication strength which must be consistently enforced across them.
Items.Evidence: docs/docs/administration documents the OAuth and password-login pathways and their enable/disable toggles, but does not document the security controls/strength that must be enforced consistently across pathways.

Items.Description: Verify that user set passwords are at least 8 characters in length although a minimum of 15 characters is strongly recommended.
Items.Evidence: ChangePasswordSchema enforces z.string().min(8) (server/src/dtos/auth.dto.ts:138); password rules covered in auth.service.spec.ts and API e2e specs.

Items.Description: Verify that users can change their password.
Items.Evidence: POST /api/auth/change-password endpoint exists (auth.controller.ts) and is covered by auth.service.spec.ts and e2e specs.

Items.Description: Verify that password change functionality requires the user's current and new password.
Items.Evidence: ChangePasswordDto requires both current password and newPassword (server/src/dtos/auth.dto.ts:134-140); asserted in auth.service.spec.ts.

Items.Description: Verify that passwords submitted during account registration or password change are checked against an available set of, at least, the top 3000 passwords which match the application's password policy, e.g. minimum length.
Items.Evidence: No check of submitted passwords against a common/top-3000 password list (no zxcvbn or blocklist dependency in server).

Items.Description: Verify that passwords of any composition can be used, without rules limiting the type of characters permitted. There must be no requirement for a minimum number of upper or lower case characters, numbers, or special characters.
Items.Evidence: The only rule is minimum length; no character-class composition requirements exist in any password schema.

Items.Description: Verify that password input fields use type=password to mask the entry. Applications may allow the user to temporarily view the entire masked password, or the last typed character of the password.
Items.Evidence: Web login and password forms use type=password (web/src/routes/auth/login/+page.svelte, settings components); no explicit test asserts this.

Items.Description: Verify that "paste" functionality, browser password helpers, and external password managers are permitted.
Items.Evidence: No paste-blocking, autocomplete=off or password-manager-hostile handlers anywhere in web/src; browsers and managers work unimpeded.

Items.Description: Verify that the application verifies the user's password exactly as received from the user, without any modifications such as truncation or case transformation.
Items.Evidence: Passwords are compared exactly as received via bcrypt compare (crypto.repository.ts compareBcrypt); no truncation, trimming or case transformation in the login/change-password paths.

Items.Description: Verify that passwords of at least 64 characters are permitted.
Items.Evidence: Password schemas have no maximum length (z.string().min(8)), so 64+ character passwords are accepted.

Items.Description: Verify that a user's password stays valid until it is discovered to be compromised or the user rotates it. The application must not require periodic credential rotation.
Items.Evidence: No password expiry or rotation is enforced anywhere; passwords stay valid until changed by the user or reset by an admin.

Items.Description: Verify that the documented list of context specific words is used to prevent easy to guess passwords being created.
Items.Evidence: No context-specific word list is enforced at registration or password change.

Items.Description: Verify that passwords submitted during account registration or password changes are checked against a set of breached passwords.
Items.Evidence: No breached-password check (no HIBP/k-anonymity or similar) at registration or password change.

Items.Description: Verify that controls to prevent attacks such as credential stuffing and password brute force are implemented according to the application's security documentation.
Items.Evidence: No rate limiting, account lockout or throttling in the server (no @nestjs/throttler or equivalent). Only a constant-time dummy bcrypt compare prevents timing-based user enumeration (auth.service.ts login).

Items.Description: Verify that default user accounts (e.g., "root", "admin", or "sa") are not present in the application or are disabled.
Items.Evidence: No built-in default accounts: the first admin is created interactively during onboarding; setup routes are disabled once an admin exists (auth.guard.spec.ts covers this).

Items.Description: Verify that either a multi-factor authentication mechanism or a combination of single-factor authentication mechanisms, must be used in order to access the application. For L3, one of the factors must be a hardware-based authentication mechanism which provides compromise and impersonation resistance against phishing attacks while verifying the intent to authenticate by requiring a user-initiated action (such as a button press on a FIDO hardware key or a mobile phone). Relaxing any of the considerations in this requirement requires a fully documented rationale and a comprehensive set of mitigating controls.
Items.Evidence: Password-only single-factor login is allowed by default, so MFA is not mandatory. However, passkeys (WebAuthn/FIDO2, phishing-resistant) are supported as an additional authentication pathway, and OAuth can offload MFA to the IdP. Passkey flows are covered by passkey.controller.spec.ts.

Items.Description: Verify that, if the application includes multiple authentication pathways, there are no undocumented pathways and that security controls and authentication strength are enforced consistently.
Items.Evidence: Four pathways exist (password, OAuth, passkey, API key) and are documented at a high level, but strength is not enforced consistently: API keys and (depending on config) password login can bypass MFA entirely.

Items.Description: Verify that users are notified of suspicious authentication attempts (successful or unsuccessful). This may include authentication attempts from an unusual location or client, partially successful authentication (only one of multiple factors), an authentication attempt after a long period of inactivity or a successful authentication after several unsuccessful attempts.
Verify that email is not used as either a single-factor or multi-factor authentication mechanism.
Verify that users are notified after updates to authentication details, such as credential resets or modification of the username or email address.

Verify that valid users cannot be deduced from failed authentication challenges, such as by basing on error messages, HTTP response codes, or different response times. Registration and forgot password functionality must also have this protection.

Verify that system generated initial passwords or activation codes are securely randomly generated, follow the existing password policy, and expire after a short period of time or after they are initially used. These initial secrets must not be permitted to become the long term password.
Items.Evidence: CLI bootstrap admin password is generated with randomBytes(24) (cli.service.ts) and meets the length policy, but there is no expiry after first use or time limit. Covered by cli.service.spec.ts.

Items.Description: Verify that password hints or knowledge-based authentication (so-called "secret questions") are not present.
Items.Evidence: No password hints or knowledge-based secret questions exist anywhere in the schema, DTOs or UI.

Items.Description: Verify that a secure process for resetting a forgotten password is implemented, that does not bypass any enabled multi-factor authentication mechanisms.
Items.Evidence: No self-service 'forgot password' email flow exists; a forgotten password is handled by an admin resetting it (user-admin service / CLI), which cannot bypass MFA since MFA is delegated to passkeys/IdP. No automated reset token exists at all.

Items.Description: Verify that if a multi-factor authentication factor is lost, evidence of identity proofing is performed at the same level as during enrollment.
Items.Evidence: The only additional factor is a passkey; losing it falls back to password or OAuth login (or admin intervention) without an identity-proofing process at the enrollment level.

Items.Description: Verify that renewal instructions for authentication mechanisms which expire are sent with enough time to be carried out before the old authentication mechanism expires, configuring automated reminders if necessary.

Verify that administrative users can initiate the password reset process for the user, but that this does not allow them to change or choose the user's password. This prevents a situation where they know the user's password.
Verify that lookup secrets, out-of-band authentication requests or codes, and time-based one-time passwords (TOTPs) are only successfully usable once.
Items.Evidence: Immich's lookup secrets (shared-link keys, API keys) are long-lived by design and not single-use; no one-time lookup secrets or OTP codes exist in the application.

Items.Description: Verify that, when being stored in the application's backend, lookup secrets with less than 112 bits of entropy (19 random alphanumeric characters or 34 random digits) are hashed with an approved password storage hashing algorithm that incorporates a 32-bit random salt. A standard hash function can be used if the secret has 112 bits of entropy or more.
Items.Evidence: Shared-link keys are generated with randomBytes(50) = 400 bits of entropy (shared-link.service.ts), well above the 112-bit threshold, but they are stored raw (unhashed) in the database instead of hashed.

Items.Description: Verify that lookup secrets, out-of-band authentication code, and time-based one-time password seeds, are generated using a Cryptographically Secure Pseudorandom Number Generator (CSPRNG) to avoid predictable values.
Items.Evidence: All lookup secrets (shared-link keys randomBytes(50), API keys randomBytes(32), session tokens randomBytes(32)) are generated with node crypto CSPRNG.

Items.Description: Verify that lookup secrets and out-of-band authentication codes have a minimum of 20 bits of entropy (typically 4 random alphanumeric characters or 6 random digits is sufficient).
Items.Evidence: Shared-link keys carry 400 bits of entropy and API keys 256 bits, far above the 20-bit minimum.

Items.Description: Verify that out-of-band authentication requests, codes, or tokens, as well as time-based one-time passwords (TOTPs) have a defined lifetime. Out of band requests must have a maximum lifetime of 10 minutes and for TOTP a maximum lifetime of 30 seconds.
Items.Evidence: Shared links support an optional expiry timestamp (and admins can enforce a maximum lifetime), but expiry is optional and defaults to none; there are no OTP/TOTP lifetimes since no OTP mechanism exists.

Items.Description: Verify that any authentication factor (including physical devices) can be revoked in case of theft or other loss.
Verify that biometric authentication mechanisms are only used as secondary factors together with either something you have or something you know.
Verify that time-based one-time passwords (TOTPs) are checked based on a time source from a trusted service and not from an untrusted or client provided time.

Verify that authentication mechanisms using the Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN) to deliver One-time Passwords (OTPs) via phone or SMS are offered only when the phone number has previously been validated, alternate stronger methods (such as Time based One-time Passwords) are also offered, and the service provides information on their security risks to users. For L3 applications, phone and SMS must not be available as options.
Items.Evidence: No PSTN/SMS/phone-based authentication exists.

Items.Description: Verify that out-of-band authentication requests, codes, or tokens are bound to the original authentication request for which they were generated and are not usable for a previous or subsequent one.
Items.Evidence: No out-of-band authentication mechanisms exist.

Items.Description: Verify that a code based out-of-band authentication mechanism is protected against brute force attacks by using rate limiting. Consider also using a code with at least 64 bits of entropy.
Items.Evidence: No out-of-band authentication codes exist.

Items.Description: Verify that, where push notifications are used for multi-factor authentication, rate limiting is used to prevent push bombing attacks. Number matching may also mitigate this risk.
Verify that the certificates used to verify cryptographic authentication assertions are stored in a way protects them from modification.
Verify that the challenge nonce is at least 64 bits in length, and statistically unique or unique over the lifetime of the cryptographic device.

Verify that, if the application supports multiple identity providers (IdPs), the user's identity cannot be spoofed via another supported identity provider (eg. by using the same user identifier). The standard mitigation would be for the application to register and identify the user using a combination of the IdP ID (serving as a namespace) and the user's ID in the IdP.
Items.Evidence: Only a single external IdP can be configured; OAuth identities are bound per user via a unique oauthId, so cross-IdP identity spoofing is not possible in this configuration.

Items.Description: Verify that the presence and integrity of digital signatures on authentication assertions (for example on JWTs or SAML assertions) are always validated, rejecting any assertions that are unsigned or have invalid signatures.
Items.Evidence: OIDC ID tokens are validated by openid-client / jose: signature via the IdP's JWKS or client secret, issuer and audience are checked (oauth.repository.ts; validateLogoutToken validates signature, iss, aud explicitly for logout tokens).

Items.Description: Verify that SAML assertions are uniquely processed and used only once within the validity period to prevent replay attacks.
Items.Evidence: No SAML support; only OIDC via openid-client.

Items.Description: Verify that, if an application uses a separate Identity Provider (IdP) and expects specific authentication strength, methods, or recentness for specific functions, the application verifies this using the information returned by the IdP. For example, if OIDC is used, this might be achieved by validating ID Token claims such as 'acr', 'amr', and 'auth_time' (if present). If the IdP does not provide this information, the application must have a documented fallback approach that assumes that the minimum strength authentication mechanism was used (for example, single-factor authentication using username and password).
Items.Evidence: No acr/amr/auth_time claim validation is performed when accepting OIDC logins; the app assumes the IdP-enforced strength (no documented fallback either).

Items.Description: Verify that the user's session inactivity timeout and absolute maximum session lifetime are documented, are appropriate in combination with other controls, and that the documentation includes justification for any deviations from NIST SP 800-63B re-authentication requirements.
Items.Evidence: Session lifetimes are not documented: sessions have no inactivity timeout and no absolute maximum lifetime (cookie maxAge 400 days, session rows persist until logout).

Items.Description: Verify that the documentation defines how many concurrent (parallel) sessions are allowed for one account as well as the intended behaviors and actions to be taken when the maximum number of active sessions is reached.
Items.Evidence: Concurrent sessions are unbounded and the policy/behavior on reaching a maximum is not documented (there is no maximum).

Items.Description: Verify that all systems that create and manage user sessions as part of a federated identity management ecosystem (such as SSO systems) are documented along with controls to coordinate session lifetimes, termination, and any other conditions that require re-authentication.
Items.Evidence: SSO session coordination is not documented: OAuth logout/backchannel logout are implemented, but lifetime coordination and re-authentication conditions are not documented.

Items.Description: Verify that the application performs all session token verification using a trusted, backend service.
Items.Evidence: Session tokens are validated server-side: AuthGuard hashes the presented token and looks up the session row in Postgres (auth.service.ts validateSession; middleware/auth.guard.ts). Covered by auth.guard.spec.ts and session e2e specs.

Items.Description: Verify that the application uses either self-contained or reference tokens that are dynamically generated for session management, i.e. not using static API secrets and keys.
Items.Evidence: Each login generates a fresh random reference token stored hashed in the session table (base.service.ts createLoginResponse). Static API keys exist but are an explicit opt-in separate credential, not the session mechanism.

Items.Description: Verify that if reference tokens are used to represent user sessions, they are unique and generated using a cryptographically secure pseudo-random number generator (CSPRNG) and possess at least 128 bits of entropy.
Items.Evidence: Session tokens are randomBytes(32) base64-encoded (>=128 bits entropy) from node crypto CSPRNG; only the SHA-256 hash is stored. Token format asserted in api-key/session specs; entropy is by construction, not measured by tests.

Items.Description: Verify that the application generates a new session token on user authentication, including re-authentication, and terminates the current session token.
Items.Evidence: A new session token is created on every authentication, but previously issued sessions for the same user are not terminated on re-login; password change offers invalidateSessions as an opt-in.

Items.Description: Verify that there is an inactivity timeout such that re-authentication is enforced according to risk analysis and documented security decisions.
Items.Evidence: No inactivity timeout exists; sessions remain valid indefinitely regardless of last use (only cookie maxAge applies client-side).

Items.Description: Verify that there is an absolute maximum session lifetime such that re-authentication is enforced according to risk analysis and documented security decisions.
Items.Evidence: No absolute maximum session lifetime is enforced; session rows have no expiry timestamp.

Items.Description: Verify that when session termination is triggered (such as logout or expiration), the application disallows any further use of the session. For reference tokens or stateful sessions, this means invalidating the session data at the application backend. Applications using self-contained tokens will need a solution such as maintaining a list of terminated tokens, disallowing tokens produced before a per-user date and time or rotating a per-user signing key.
Items.Evidence: Logout deletes the session row server-side (auth.service.ts logout -> sessionRepository.delete); the token is unusable afterwards. Covered by auth.service.spec.ts and e2e session specs.

Items.Description: Verify that the application terminates all active sessions when a user account is disabled or deleted (such as an employee leaving the company).
Items.Evidence: Sessions are FK-cascade deleted with the user (session.table.ts onDelete: CASCADE), so account deletion removes sessions; password change can invalidate all sessions (invalidateSessions flag). Merely disabling a user does not proactively kill existing sessions.

Items.Description: Verify that the application gives the option to terminate all other active sessions after a successful change or removal of any authentication factor (including password change via reset or recovery and, if present, an MFA settings update).
Items.Evidence: Password change exposes an opt-in invalidateSessions flag (default false) that revokes all other sessions; passkey setup/reset does not terminate other sessions. Covered by auth.service.spec.ts.

Items.Description: Verify that all pages that require authentication have easy and visible access to logout functionality.
Items.Evidence: Every authenticated web page has the account menu with logout, and a dedicated sessions page lists and terminates individual sessions; mobile apps expose logout. Covered by web auth e2e.

Items.Description: Verify that application administrators are able to terminate active sessions for an individual user or for all users.
Items.Evidence: Admins can list a user's sessions (user-admin.service.ts) and deleting the user cascades sessions, but there is no admin endpoint to revoke an individual user's sessions without deleting the account.

Items.Description: Verify that the application requires full re-authentication before allowing modifications to sensitive account attributes which may affect authentication such as email address, phone number, MFA configuration, or other information used in account recovery.
Items.Evidence: Sensitive account changes such as email update (UserUpdateMeDto) do not require re-authentication or the current password; only the password change itself does.

Items.Description: Verify that users are able to view and (having authenticated again with at least one factor) terminate any or all currently active sessions.
Items.Evidence: The sessions UI lists all active devices/sessions for the logged-in user and allows terminating any or all of them; covered by session e2e specs and session.service specs.

Items.Description: Verify that the application requires further authentication with at least one factor or secondary verification before performing highly sensitive transactions or operations.

Verify that session lifetime and termination between Relying Parties (RPs) and Identity Providers (IdPs) behave as documented, requiring re-authentication as necessary such as when the maximum time between IdP authentication events is reached.
Items.Evidence: RP/IdP session behavior is implemented (logout with id_token_hint, OAuth backchannel logout invalidating sessions by sid/sub) but the lifetime coordination policy is not documented and no re-authentication window is enforced.

Items.Description: Verify that creation of a session requires either the user's consent or an explicit action, preventing the creation of new application sessions without user interaction.
Items.Evidence: Sessions are only created on explicit login actions (credential login, OAuth callback, passkey ceremony); no mechanism creates sessions without user interaction.

Items.Description: Verify that authorization documentation defines rules for restricting function-level and data-specific access based on consumer permissions and resource attributes.
Items.Evidence: There is no authorization documentation in docs/ defining function-level and data-level rules; the model exists only in code (Permission enum, access repository).

Items.Description: Verify that authorization documentation defines rules for field-level access restrictions (both read and write) based on consumer permissions and resource attributes. Note that these rules might depend on other attribute values of the relevant data object, such as state or status.
Items.Evidence: No documentation defines field-level read/write rules; field-level differences exist only implicitly in DTO mappers (mapUser vs mapUserAdmin).

Items.Description: Verify that the application's documentation defines the environmental and contextual attributes (including but not limited to, time of day, user location, IP address, or device) that are used in the application to make security decisions, including those pertaining to authentication and authorization.

Verify that authentication and authorization documentation defines how environmental and contextual factors are used in decision-making, in addition to function-level, data-specific, and field-level authorization. This should include the attributes evaluated, thresholds for risk, and actions taken (e.g., allow, challenge, deny, step-up authentication).
Verify that the application ensures that function-level access is restricted to consumers with explicit permissions.
Items.Evidence: Routes are guarded by @Authenticated({ admin, permission }) with a central Permission enum checked in AuthGuard (middleware/auth.guard.ts); covered by auth.guard.spec.ts and controller specs.

Items.Description: Verify that the application ensures that data-specific access is restricted to consumers with explicit permissions to specific data items to mitigate insecure direct object reference (IDOR) and broken object level authorization (BOLA).
Items.Evidence: Data-level access is enforced via the access repository (owner/partner/album/shared-link checks) for assets, albums and people; extensively covered by service specs and e2e specs (asset, album, shared-link).

Items.Description: Verify that the application ensures that field-level access is restricted to consumers with explicit permissions to specific fields to mitigate broken object property level authorization (BOPLA).
Items.Evidence: Response DTOs whitelist fields per role (admin mappers expose more than user mappers; password hashes are never mapped), but there is no fine-grained per-field permission model beyond the admin/user split.

Items.Description: Verify that adaptive security controls based on a consumer's environmental and contextual attributes (such as time of day, location, IP address, or device) are implemented for authentication and authorization decisions, as defined in the application's documentation. These controls must be applied when the consumer tries to start a new session and also during an existing session.
Verify that the application enforces authorization rules at a trusted service layer and doesn't rely on controls that an untrusted consumer could manipulate, such as client-side JavaScript.
Items.Evidence: All authorization decisions run in the NestJS server (guard + services + access repository); the web client only hides UI elements and never grants access.

Items.Description: Verify that changes to values on which authorization decisions are made are applied immediately. Where changes cannot be applied immediately, (such as when relying on data in self-contained tokens), there must be mitigating controls to alert when a consumer performs an action when they are no longer authorized to do so and revert the change. Note that this alternative would not mitigate information leakage.

Verify that access to an object is based on the originating subject's (e.g. consumer's) permissions, not on the permissions of any intermediary or service acting on their behalf. For example, if a consumer calls a web service using a self-contained token for authentication, and the service then requests data from a different service, the second service will use the consumer's token, rather than a machine-to-machine token from the first service, to make permission decisions.
Verify that multi-tenant applications use cross-tenant controls to ensure consumer operations will never affect tenants with which they do not have permissions to interact.
Items.Evidence: Immich is a single-tenant self-hosted application (one instance, one photo library with per-user sharing); there is no multi-tenant surface to isolate.

Items.Description: Verify that access to administrative interfaces incorporates multiple layers of security, including continuous consumer identity verification, device security posture assessment, and contextual risk analysis, ensuring that network location or trusted endpoints are not the sole factors for authorization even though they may reduce the likelihood of unauthorized access.
Verify that self-contained tokens are validated using their digital signature or MAC to protect against tampering before accepting the token's contents.
Items.Evidence: Self-contained JWTs (workflow execution tokens) are verified with HS256 signature before use (crypto.repository.ts verifyJwt, workflow-execution.service.ts).

Items.Description: Verify that only algorithms on an allowlist can be used to create and verify self-contained tokens, for a given context. The allowlist must include the permitted algorithms, ideally only either symmetric or asymmetric algorithms, and must not include the 'None' algorithm. If both symmetric and asymmetric must be supported, additional controls will be needed to prevent key confusion.
Items.Evidence: jwt.verify is called with an explicit algorithm allowlist algorithms: ['HS256'] and signing is pinned to HS256; 'none' cannot be accepted.

Items.Description: Verify that key material that is used to validate self-contained tokens is from trusted pre-configured sources for the token issuer, preventing attackers from specifying untrusted sources and keys. For JWTs and other JWS structures, headers such as 'jku', 'x5u', and 'jwk' must be validated against an allowlist of trusted sources.
Items.Evidence: The JWT secret comes from the server's environment config only; no jku/x5u/jwk header handling exists, so untrusted key sources cannot be injected.

Items.Description: Verify that, if a validity time span is present in the token data, the token and its content are accepted only if the verification time is within this validity time span. For example, for JWTs, the claims 'nbf' and 'exp' must be verified.
Items.Evidence: Reference session tokens are validated against the DB with no client-side expiry. The self-contained workflow JWTs are signed without exp/nbf claims, so no validity timespan is enforced for them.

Items.Description: Verify that the service receiving a token validates the token to be the correct type and is meant for the intended purpose before accepting the token's contents. For example, only access tokens can be accepted for authorization decisions and only ID Tokens can be used for proving user authentication.
Items.Evidence: Session/API-key tokens are opaque reference tokens validated against their DB rows (correct purpose by construction). The self-contained workflow JWTs carry no typ claim and are not type-checked beyond algorithm and signature.

Items.Description: Verify that the service only accepts tokens which are intended for use with that service (audience). For JWTs, this can be achieved by validating the 'aud' claim against an allowlist defined in the service.
Items.Evidence: Reference tokens are inherently single-audience; however the workflow JWTs are signed without an aud claim, so an audience check is not possible for them.

Items.Description: Verify that, if a token issuer uses the same private key for issuing tokens to different audiences, the issued tokens contain an audience restriction that uniquely identifies the intended audiences. This will prevent a token from being reused with an unintended audience. If the audience identifier is dynamically provisioned, the token issuer must validate these audiences in order to make sure that they do not result in audience impersonation.
Items.Evidence: Immich does not issue tokens to multiple audiences; its JWTs are self-consumed only (and session tokens are opaque).

Items.Description: Verify that tokens are only sent to components that strictly need them. For example, when using a backend-for-frontend pattern for browser-based JavaScript applications, access and refresh tokens shall only be accessible for the backend.
Items.Evidence: Backend-for-frontend pattern: the OAuth access/refresh tokens are stored server-side on the session row (oauthBearerToken); the browser only receives the HttpOnly session cookie, never upstream tokens.

Items.Description: Verify that the client only accepts values from the authorization server (such as the authorization code or ID Token) if these values result from an authorization flow that was initiated by the same user agent session and transaction. This requires that client-generated secrets, such as the proof key for code exchange (PKCE) 'code_verifier', 'state' or OIDC 'nonce', are not guessable, are specific to the transaction, and are securely bound to both the client and the user agent session in which the transaction was started.
Items.Evidence: PKCE code_verifier and state are generated server-side with randomBytes, bound to the user agent via HttpOnly cookies (oauth.controller.ts), and verified on callback; asserted in oauth.controller.spec.ts.

Items.Description: Verify that, if the code flow is used, the OAuth client has protection against browser-based request forgery attacks, commonly known as cross-site request forgery (CSRF), which trigger token requests, either by using proof key for code exchange (PKCE) functionality or checking the 'state' parameter that was sent in the authorization request.
Items.Evidence: The OAuth client uses PKCE plus a state parameter bound to the handshake via cookies, preventing CSRF on the code flow; covered by oauth.controller.spec.ts and oauth e2e specs.

Items.Description: Verify that, if the OAuth client can interact with more than one authorization server, it has a defense against mix-up attacks. For example, it could require that the authorization server return the 'iss' parameter value and validate it in the authorization response and the token response.
Items.Evidence: Only one authorization server can be configured; mix-up attacks require multiple AS configurations.

Items.Description: Verify that the OAuth client only requests the required scopes (or other authorization parameters) in requests to the authorization server.

Verify that the resource server only accepts access tokens that are intended for use with that service (audience). The audience may be included in a structured access token (such as the 'aud' claim in JWT), or it can be checked using the token introspection endpoint.
Items.Evidence: Immich does not accept structured access tokens from an authorization server; its API credentials are opaque session tokens and API keys validated against the database, so the audience concept does not apply.

Items.Description: Verify that the resource server enforces authorization decisions based on claims from the access token that define delegated authorization. If claims such as 'sub', 'scope', and 'authorization_details' are present, they must be part of the decision.
Items.Evidence: Authorization decisions are based on the DB user/permissions behind opaque tokens, not on claims from third-party access tokens.

Items.Description: Verify that if an access control decision requires identifying a unique user from an access token (JWT or related token introspection response), the resource server identifies the user from claims that cannot be reassigned to other users. Typically, it means using a combination of 'iss' and 'sub' claims.
Items.Evidence: User identity comes from the session/API-key row (immutable UUID), not from claims in access tokens that could be reassigned.
