Items.Description: Verify that, if the resource server requires specific authentication strength, methods, or recentness, it verifies that the presented access token satisfies these constraints. For example, if present, using the OIDC 'acr', 'amr' and 'auth_time' claims respectively.
Items.Evidence: No acr/amr/auth_time constraints are verified for any presented credential; if MFA strength matters, it must be enforced at the (single) IdP.

Items.Description: Verify that the resource server prevents the use of stolen access tokens or replay of access tokens (from unauthorized parties) by requiring sender-constrained access tokens, either Mutual TLS for OAuth 2 or OAuth 2 Demonstration of Proof of Possession (DPoP).
Verify that the authorization server validates redirect URIs based on a client-specific allowlist of pre-registered URIs using exact string comparison.
Items.Evidence: Immich is an OAuth client, not an authorization server; it consumes external OIDC providers via openid-client and never issues authorization codes.

Items.Description: Verify that, if the authorization server returns the authorization code in the authorization response, it can be used only once for a token request. For the second valid request with an authorization code that has already been used to issue an access token, the authorization server must reject a token request and revoke any issued tokens related to the authorization code.
Items.Evidence: Not an authorization server; no authorization codes are issued by Immich.

Items.Description: Verify that the authorization code is short-lived. The maximum lifetime can be up to 10 minutes for L1 and L2 applications and up to 1 minute for L3 applications.
Items.Evidence: Not an authorization server; no authorization codes are issued by Immich.

Items.Description: Verify that for a given client, the authorization server only allows the usage of grants that this client needs to use. Note that the grants 'token' (Implicit flow) and 'password' (Resource Owner Password Credentials flow) must no longer be used.
Items.Evidence: Not an authorization server; Immich only performs the authorization-code + PKCE flow as a client.

Items.Description: Verify that the authorization server mitigates refresh token replay attacks for public clients, preferably using sender-constrained refresh tokens, i.e., Demonstrating Proof of Possession (DPoP) or Certificate-Bound Access Tokens using mutual TLS (mTLS). For L1 and L2 applications, refresh token rotation may be used. If refresh token rotation is used, the authorization server must invalidate the refresh token after usage, and revoke all refresh tokens for that authorization if an already used and invalidated refresh token is provided.
Items.Evidence: Not an authorization server; refresh tokens of the upstream provider are stored server-side per session, never exposed to browser clients.

Items.Description: Verify that, if the code grant is used, the authorization server mitigates authorization code interception attacks by requiring proof key for code exchange (PKCE). For authorization requests, the authorization server must require a valid 'code_challenge' value and must not accept a 'code_challenge_method' value of 'plain'. For a token request, it must require validation of the 'code_verifier' parameter.
Items.Evidence: Not an authorization server; PKCE is used on the client side only.

Items.Description: Verify that if the authorization server supports unauthenticated dynamic client registration, it mitigates the risk of malicious client applications. It must validate client metadata such as any registered URIs, ensure the user's consent, and warn the user before processing an authorization request with an untrusted client application.
Items.Evidence: Not an authorization server; no dynamic client registration is performed or offered.

Items.Description: Verify that refresh tokens have an absolute expiration, including if sliding refresh token expiration is applied.
Items.Evidence: Not an authorization server; refresh tokens belong to the upstream IdP and are only stored/revoked by Immich.

Items.Description: Verify that refresh tokens and reference access tokens can be revoked by an authorized user using the authorization server user interface, to mitigate the risk of malicious clients or stolen tokens.
Items.Evidence: Not an authorization server; Immich has no token revocation UI for upstream tokens (session deletion drops the stored bearer token).

Items.Description: Verify that confidential client is authenticated for client-to-authorized server backchannel requests such as token requests, pushed authorization requests (PAR), and token revocation requests.
Items.Evidence: Not an authorization server; backchannel requests to the IdP authenticate with the configured client credentials.

Items.Description: Verify that the authorization server configuration only assigns the required scopes to the OAuth client.
Items.Evidence: Not an authorization server; scope assignment is an IdP-side concern.

Items.Description: Verify that for a given client, the authorization server only allows the 'response_mode' value that this client needs to use. For example, by having the authorization server validate this value against the expected values or by using pushed authorization request (PAR) or JWT-secured Authorization Request (JAR).
Verify that grant type 'code' is always used together with pushed authorization requests (PAR).

Verify that the authorization server issues only sender-constrained (Proof-of-Possession) access tokens, either with certificate-bound access tokens using mutual TLS (mTLS) or DPoP-bound access tokens (Demonstration of Proof of Possession).

Verify that, for a server-side client (which is not executed on the end-user device), the authorization server ensures that the 'authorization_details' parameter value is from the client backend and that the user has not tampered with it. For example, by requiring the usage of pushed authorization request (PAR) or JWT-secured Authorization Request (JAR).

Verify that the client is confidential and the authorization server requires the use of strong client authentication methods (based on public-key cryptography and resistant to replay attacks), such as mutual TLS ('tls_client_auth', 'self_signed_tls_client_auth') or private key JWT ('private_key_jwt').

Verify that the client (as the relying party) mitigates ID Token replay attacks. For example, by ensuring that the 'nonce' claim in the ID Token matches the 'nonce' value sent in the authentication request to the OpenID Provider (in OAuth2 refereed to as the authorization request sent to the authorization server).
Items.Evidence: The OIDC client (openid-client) generates and validates a nonce per authentication request, binding the ID token to the original request.

Items.Description: Verify that the client uniquely identifies the user from ID Token claims, usually the 'sub' claim, which cannot be reassigned to other users (for the scope of an identity provider).
Items.Evidence: Users are identified by the IdP's sub claim stored as a unique oauthId per user; emails may link accounts but the sub-based binding is not reassignable within the IdP.

Items.Description: Verify that the client rejects attempts by a malicious authorization server to impersonate another authorization server through authorization server metadata. The client must reject authorization server metadata if the issuer URL in the authorization server metadata does not exactly match the pre-configured issuer URL expected by the client.
Items.Evidence: openid-client validates the issuer in the server metadata against the pre-configured issuerUrl (new URL(issuerUrl) in oauth.repository.ts); metadata from a different issuer is rejected.

Items.Description: Verify that the client validates that the ID Token is intended to be used for that client (audience) by checking that the 'aud' claim from the token is equal to the 'client_id' value for the client.
Items.Evidence: openid-client validates the ID token aud claim against the configured clientId before accepting the login.

Items.Description: Verify that, when using OIDC back-channel logout, the relying party mitigates denial of service through forced logout and cross-JWT confusion in the logout flow. The client must verify that the logout token is correctly typed with a value of 'logout+jwt', contains the 'event' claim with the correct member name, and does not contain a 'nonce' claim. Note that it is also recommended to have a short expiration (e.g., 2 minutes).
Items.Evidence: Backchannel logout tokens are validated for signature, issuer, audience, maxTokenAge 2m, presence of the backchannel-logout event claim and absence of nonce (oauth.repository.ts validateLogoutToken); the typ='logout+jwt' claim is not checked.

Items.Description: Verify that the OpenID Provider only allows values 'code', 'ciba', 'id_token', or 'id_token code' for response mode. Note that 'code' is preferred over 'id_token code' (the OIDC Hybrid flow), and 'token' (any Implicit flow) must not be used.
Items.Evidence: Immich is not an OpenID Provider; response modes are a property of the upstream IdP.

Items.Description: Verify that the OpenID Provider mitigates denial of service through forced logout. By obtaining explicit confirmation from the end-user or, if present, validating parameters in the logout request (initiated by the relying party), such as the 'id_token_hint'.
Items.Evidence: Immich is not an OpenID Provider and does not host user sessions for relying parties.

Items.Description: Verify that the authorization server ensures that the user consents to each authorization request. If the identity of the client cannot be assured, the authorization server must always explicitly prompt the user for consent.
Items.Evidence: Immich is not an authorization server; consent screens are the IdP's responsibility.

Items.Description: Verify that when the authorization server prompts for user consent, it presents sufficient and clear information about what is being consented to. When applicable, this should include the nature of the requested authorizations (typically based on scope, resource server, Rich Authorization Requests (RAR) authorization details), the identity of the authorized application, and the lifetime of these authorizations.
Items.Evidence: Immich is not an authorization server; no consent prompts are rendered.

Items.Description: Verify that the user can review, modify, and revoke consents which the user has granted through the authorization server.
Items.Evidence: Immich is not an authorization server; there are no user-consented grants to review.

Items.Description: Verify that there is a documented policy for management of cryptographic keys and a cryptographic key lifecycle that follows a key management standard such as NIST SP 800-57. This should include ensuring that keys are not overshared (for example, with more than two entities for shared secrets and more than one entity for private keys).
Items.Evidence: No key-management policy exists; the JWT secret and OAuth client secret are single shared secrets provided via environment variables without documented lifecycle, rotation or sharing limits.

Items.Description: Verify that a cryptographic inventory is performed, maintained, regularly updated, and includes all cryptographic keys, algorithms, and certificates used by the application. It must also document where keys can and cannot be used in the system, and the types of data that can and cannot be protected using the keys.
Items.Evidence: No cryptographic inventory exists; the keys in use (JWT secret, OAuth client secret, license public keys) and algorithms (bcrypt, SHA-256, HS256) are only discoverable from code.

Items.Description: Verify that cryptographic discovery mechanisms are employed to identify all instances of cryptography in the system, including encryption, hashing, and signing operations.

Verify that a cryptographic inventory is maintained. This must include a documented plan that outlines the migration path to new cryptographic standards, such as post-quantum cryptography, in order to react to future threats.
Verify that industry-validated implementations (including libraries and hardware-accelerated implementations) are used for cryptographic operations.
Items.Evidence: All crypto uses industry-validated implementations: node crypto (OpenSSL), bcrypt, jose/openid-client for JWT/OIDC; no hand-rolled cryptography.

Items.Description: Verify that the application is designed with crypto agility such that random number, authenticated encryption, MAC, or hashing algorithms, key lengths, rounds, ciphers and modes can be reconfigured, upgraded, or swapped at any time, to protect against cryptographic breaks. Similarly, it must also be possible to replace keys and passwords and re-encrypt data. This will allow for seamless upgrades to post-quantum cryptography (PQC), once high-assurance implementations of approved PQC schemes or standards are widely available.
Items.Evidence: Algorithms and key lengths are fixed in code (bcrypt cost 10, HS256, SHA-256) with no reconfiguration or swap mechanism; keys can be rotated via env but no crypto-agility design exists.

Items.Description: Verify that all cryptographic primitives utilize a minimum of 128-bits of security based on the algorithm, key size, and configuration. For example, a 256-bit ECC key provides roughly 128 bits of security where RSA requires a 3072-bit key to achieve 128 bits of security.
Items.Evidence: All primitives meet the 128-bit bar: SHA-256 and HS256 (256-bit), bcrypt (adaptive, up to 72-byte passwords), CSPRNG tokens of 256-400 bits.

Items.Description: Verify that all cryptographic operations are constant-time, with no 'short-circuit' operations in comparisons, calculations, or returns, to avoid leaking information.
Verify that all cryptographic modules fail securely, and errors are handled in a way that does not enable vulnerabilities, such as Padding Oracle attacks.
Verify that insecure block modes (e.g., ECB) and weak padding schemes (e.g., PKCS#1 v1.5) are not used.
Items.Evidence: No direct block-cipher usage in server code; only bcrypt (passwords) and SHA-256 (token hashing) are used, so no ECB mode or PKCS#1 v1.5 padding appears.

Items.Description: Verify that only approved ciphers and modes such as AES with GCM are used.
Items.Evidence: No bulk encryption is implemented in application code; at-rest encryption is delegated to the database/storage layer, and the only crypto primitives used are bcrypt and SHA-256.

Items.Description: Verify that encrypted data is protected against unauthorized modification preferably by using an approved authenticated encryption method or by combining an approved encryption method with an approved MAC algorithm.
Items.Evidence: The application does not encrypt data at the application layer; at-rest encryption is delegated to the database/storage layer, so there is no app-level ciphertext to integrity-protect.

Items.Description: Verify that nonces, initialization vectors, and other single-use numbers are not used for more than one encryption key and data-element pair. The method of generation must be appropriate for the algorithm being used.
Verify that any combination of an encryption algorithm and a MAC algorithm is operating in encrypt-then-MAC mode.

Verify that only approved hash functions are used for general cryptographic use cases, including digital signatures, HMAC, KDF, and random bit generation. Disallowed hash functions, such as MD5, must not be used for any cryptographic purpose.
Items.Evidence: SHA-256 (token/session hashing) and bcrypt are the only security hashes; SHA-1 is used solely for asset dedup checksums, a non-security purpose.

Items.Description: Verify that passwords are stored using an approved, computationally intensive, key derivation function (also known as a "password hashing function"), with parameter settings configured based on current guidance. The settings should balance security and performance to make brute-force attacks sufficiently challenging for the required level of security.
Items.Evidence: Passwords and PIN codes are hashed with bcrypt at cost 10 (SALT_ROUNDS in constants.ts, hashBcrypt in crypto.repository.ts); an approved password-hashing function, though 10 is the lower bound of current guidance. Asserted in auth/user service specs.

Items.Description: Verify that hash functions used in digital signatures, as part of data authentication or data integrity are collision resistant and have appropriate bit-lengths. If collision resistance is required, the output length must be at least 256 bits. If only resistance to second pre-image attacks is required, the output length must be at least 128 bits.
Items.Evidence: SHA-256 (256-bit) is used for token hashing and integrity; bcrypt (with salt) for passwords. SHA-1 appears only for non-security asset checksums.

Items.Description: Verify that the application uses approved key derivation functions with key stretching parameters when deriving secret keys from passwords. The parameters in use must balance security and performance to prevent brute-force attacks from compromising the resulting cryptographic key.
Items.Evidence: No secret keys are derived from passwords; the only password-based derivations are bcrypt hashes for storage (PIN codes likewise), which is the approved use.

Items.Description: Verify that all random numbers and strings which are intended to be non-guessable must be generated using a cryptographically secure pseudo-random number generator (CSPRNG) and have at least 128 bits of entropy. Note that UUIDs do not respect this condition.
Items.Evidence: All security-relevant random values use node crypto CSPRNG with at least 128 bits (session/API keys 32 bytes, shared-link keys 50 bytes, OAuth state/verifier); UUIDs are used only for entity identifiers, not as secrets.

Items.Description: Verify that the random number generation mechanism in use is designed to work securely, even under heavy demand.

Verify that only approved cryptographic algorithms and modes of operation are used for key generation and seeding, and digital signature generation and verification. Key generation algorithms must not generate insecure keys vulnerable to known attacks, for example, RSA keys which are vulnerable to Fermat factorization.
Items.Evidence: Only HS256 JWTs with env-provided secrets and pinned RSA public keys for license verification are used; no key generation is performed in application code.

Items.Description: Verify that approved cryptographic algorithms are used for key exchange (such as Diffie-Hellman) with a focus on ensuring that key exchange mechanisms use secure parameters. This will prevent attacks on the key establishment process which could lead to adversary-in-the-middle attacks or cryptographic breaks.
Verify that full memory encryption is in use that protects sensitive data while it is in use, preventing access by unauthorized users or processes.
Verify that data minimization ensures the minimal amount of data is exposed during processing, and ensure that data is encrypted immediately after use or as soon as feasible.
Verify that only the latest recommended versions of the TLS protocol are enabled, such as TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3. The latest version of the TLS protocol must be the preferred option.
Items.Evidence: The application itself listens on plain HTTP; TLS protocol versions and preference are determined by the reverse proxy / deployment environment, which the docs require but the app neither enforces nor tests.

Items.Description: Verify that only recommended cipher suites are enabled, with the strongest cipher suites set as preferred. L3 applications must only support cipher suites which provide forward secrecy.
Items.Evidence: Cipher suite selection is a reverse-proxy/deployment concern; the app does not terminate TLS and pins no cipher suites.

Items.Description: Verify that the application validates that mTLS client certificates are trusted before using the certificate identity for authentication or authorization.
Items.Evidence: mTLS client-certificate authentication is not used anywhere in the application or its documented deployments.

Items.Description: Verify that proper certification revocation, such as Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) Stapling, is enabled and configured.

Verify that Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) is enabled in the application's TLS settings to prevent exposure of sensitive metadata, such as the Server Name Indication (SNI), during TLS handshake processes.

Items.Name: HTTPS Communication with External Facing Services

Items.Description: Verify that TLS is used for all connectivity between a client and external facing, HTTP-based services, and does not fall back to insecure or unencrypted communications.
Items.Evidence: No TLS code or HTTP->HTTPS fallback exists in the app; secure transport is a deployment responsibility (reverse proxy per docs/docs/install). Cookies are marked Secure only when the incoming connection is trusted as secure.

Items.Description: Verify that external facing services use publicly trusted TLS certificates.
Items.Evidence: Certificate issuance/trust is entirely outside the codebase (self-hosted deployments choose their own reverse proxy certificates); not verifiable from the project.

Items.Name: General Service to Service Communication Security

Items.Description: Verify that an encrypted protocol such as TLS is used for all inbound and outbound connections to and from the application, including monitoring systems, management tools, remote access and SSH, middleware, databases, mainframes, partner systems, or external APIs. The server must not fall back to insecure or unencrypted protocols.
Items.Evidence: Postgres supports configurable sslmode (DB_SSL_MODE), but Redis and the ML service are reached over plain HTTP/TCP on the internal Docker network by default; no end-to-end encryption policy exists.

Items.Description: Verify that TLS clients validate certificates received before communicating with a TLS server.
Items.Evidence: Outbound TLS validation is delegated: node fetch validates certificates for https endpoints (version check, IdP metadata); the DB sslmode default does not enforce certificate validation.

Items.Description: Verify that TLS or another appropriate transport encryption mechanism used for all connectivity between internal, HTTP-based services within the application, and does not fall back to insecure or unencrypted communications.
Items.Evidence: Internal HTTP-based services (ML server, Redis, Postgres) communicate unencrypted on the container network by default; TLS is not configured between them.

Items.Description: Verify that TLS connections between internal services use trusted certificates. Where internally generated or self-signed certificates are used, the consuming service must be configured to only trust specific internal CAs and specific self-signed certificates.
Items.Evidence: No internal TLS trust configuration exists (no internal CA or pinned self-signed certificates); internal traffic is plaintext by default.

Items.Description: Verify that services communicating internally within a system (intra-service communications) use strong authentication to ensure that each endpoint is verified. Strong authentication methods, such as TLS client authentication, must be employed to ensure identity, using public-key infrastructure and mechanisms that are resistant to replay attacks. For microservice architectures, consider using a service mesh to simplify certificate management and enhance security.

Verify that all communication needs for the application are documented. This must include external services which the application relies upon and cases where an end user might be able to provide an external location to which the application will then connect.
Items.Evidence: docs describe the deployment architecture (Postgres, Redis, ML server, reverse proxy, map tiles/version-check endpoints), but there is no complete, consolidated communication inventory.

Items.Description: Verify that for each service the application uses, the documentation defines the maximum number of concurrent connections (e.g., connection pool limits) and how the application behaves when that limit is reached, including any fallback or recovery mechanisms, to prevent denial of service conditions.

Verify that the application documentation defines resource‑management strategies for every external system or service it uses (e.g., databases, file handles, threads, HTTP connections). This should include resource‑release procedures, timeout settings, failure handling, and where retry logic is implemented, specifying retry limits, delays, and back‑off algorithms. For synchronous HTTP request–response operations it should mandate short timeouts and either disable retries or strictly limit retries to prevent cascading delays and resource exhaustion.

Verify that the application's documentation defines the secrets that are critical for the security of the application and a schedule for rotating them, based on the organization's threat model and business requirements.

Verify that communications between backend application components that don't support the application's standard user session mechanism, including APIs, middleware, and data layers, are authenticated. Authentication must use individual service accounts, short-term tokens, or certificate-based authentication and not unchanging credentials such as passwords, API keys, or shared accounts with privileged access.
Items.Evidence: Backend services authenticate with individual credentials: Postgres/Redis use credentials from environment variables per deployment; however these are static shared passwords rather than short-term tokens or certificates.

Items.Description: Verify that communications between backend application components, including local or operating system services, APIs, middleware, and data layers, are performed with accounts assigned the least necessary privileges.
Items.Evidence: The application uses a single DB owner account (needed for migrations) rather than least-privilege per-service accounts; Redis access is unprivileged.

Items.Description: Verify that if a credential has to be used for service authentication, the credential being used by the consumer is not a default credential (e.g., root/root or admin/admin).
Items.Evidence: No default credentials are compiled in or shipped: docker-compose requires DB/Redis passwords via environment variables; example env files contain placeholders, not working credentials.

Items.Description: Verify that an allowlist is used to define the external resources or systems with which the application is permitted to communicate (e.g., for outbound requests, data loads, or file access). This allowlist can be implemented at the application layer, web server, firewall, or a combination of different layers.
Items.Evidence: No outbound allowlist exists; the server fetches admin-configured URLs (ML endpoint, map/reverse-geocode URLs, OAuth issuer) without allowlist validation.

Items.Description: Verify that the web or application server is configured with an allowlist of resources or systems to which the server can send requests or load data or files from.
Items.Evidence: No allowlist restricts outbound destinations at the application layer; only fixed constants (version check) and admin-configured URLs are fetched.

Items.Description: Verify that where the application connects to separate services, it follows the documented configuration for each connection, such as maximum parallel connections, behavior when maximum allowed connections is reached, connection timeouts, and retry strategies.

Verify that a secrets management solution, such as a key vault, is used to securely create, store, control access to, and destroy backend secrets. These could include passwords, key material, integrations with databases and third-party systems, keys and seeds for time-based tokens, other internal secrets, and API keys. Secrets must not be included in application source code or included in build artifacts. For an L3 application, this must involve a hardware-backed solution such as an HSM.
Items.Evidence: Secrets are supplied via environment variables (no secrets in source code or build artifacts); there is no vault/KMS integration, and JWT/OAuth secrets are long-lived shared secrets.

Items.Description: Verify that access to secret assets adheres to the principle of least privilege.
Items.Evidence: Access to secrets is limited to the server process/container (env vars, docker secrets pattern), but no formal least-privilege access model for secret assets is documented or enforced.

Items.Description: Verify that all cryptographic operations are performed using an isolated security module (such as a vault or hardware security module) to securely manage and protect key material from exposure outside of the security module.
Verify that secrets are configured to expire and be rotated based on the application's documentation.

Verify that the application is deployed either without any source control metadata, including the .git or .svn folders, or in a way that these folders are inaccessible both externally and to the application itself.
Items.Evidence: The production Docker image COPYs only source directories and build outputs (server/Dockerfile); .git/.svn metadata is never copied into the image.

Items.Description: Verify that debug modes are disabled for all components in production environments to prevent exposure of debugging features and information leakage.
Items.Evidence: Production mode disables dev CORS and Swagger spec writing, and log levels are configurable; however the Swagger UI remains mounted in production unless disabled, and debug logging can be enabled via env.

Items.Description: Verify that web servers do not expose directory listings to clients unless explicitly intended.
Items.Evidence: Static file serving uses sirv without directory listings (app.common.ts); only built assets and API routes are reachable.

Items.Description: Verify that using the HTTP TRACE method is not supported in production environments, to avoid potential information leakage.
Items.Evidence: Node's HTTP server does not implement the TRACE method; such requests are rejected (404) by Express in all environments.

Items.Description: Verify that documentation (such as for internal APIs) and monitoring endpoints are not exposed unless explicitly intended.
Items.Evidence: Monitoring endpoints are opt-in: the /api/metrics endpoint requires telemetry to be enabled via env; however Swagger/OpenAPI documentation endpoints are exposed on the public API in production.

Items.Description: Verify that the application does not expose detailed version information of backend components.
Verify that the web tier is configured to only serve files with specific file extensions to prevent unintentional information, configuration, and source code leakage.

Verify that all sensitive data created and processed by the application has been identified and classified into protection levels. This includes data that is only encoded and therefore easily decoded, such as Base64 strings or the plaintext payload inside a JWT. Protection levels need to take into account any data protection and privacy regulations and standards which the application is required to comply with.
Items.Evidence: No data classification or protection-level inventory exists for sensitive data (photos, tokens, user PII).

Items.Description: Verify that all sensitive data protection levels have a documented set of protection requirements. This must include (but not be limited to) requirements related to general encryption, integrity verification, retention, how the data is to be logged, access controls around sensitive data in logs, database-level encryption, privacy and privacy-enhancing technologies to be used, and other confidentiality requirements.
Items.Evidence: No documented protection requirements per data class (encryption, retention, logging rules) exist.

Items.Description: Verify that sensitive data is only sent to the server in the HTTP message body or header fields, and that the URL and query string do not contain sensitive information, such as an API key or session token.
Items.Evidence: Session tokens travel in HttpOnly cookies or the Authorization header, API keys in x-api-key; however shared-link keys are secrets embedded in URLs by design (web/src/routes/(user)/share/[key]).

Items.Description: Verify that the application prevents sensitive data from being cached in server components, such as load balancers and application caches, or ensures that the data is securely purged after use.
Items.Evidence: API responses use private/no-cache Cache-Control for originals and thumbnails (server/src/utils/file.ts), limiting intermediary caching; the compression middleware still processes all responses and shared CDNs are a deployment concern.

Items.Description: Verify that defined sensitive data is not sent to untrusted parties (e.g., user trackers) to prevent unwanted collection of data outside of the application's control.
Items.Evidence: No third-party trackers or analytics are embedded; the optional telemetry feature (version check, anonymous metrics) is opt-in and documented.

Items.Description: Verify that controls around sensitive data related to encryption, integrity verification, retention, how the data is to be logged, access controls around sensitive data in logs, privacy and privacy-enhancing technologies, are implemented as defined in the documentation for the specific data's protection level.
Items.Evidence: No per-protection-level control implementation exists because no protection levels are defined.

Items.Description: Verify that caching mechanisms are configured to only cache responses which have the expected content type for that resource and do not contain sensitive, dynamic content. The web server should return a 404 or 302 response when a non-existent file is accessed rather than returning a different, valid file. This should prevent Web Cache Deception attacks.

Verify that the application only returns the minimum required sensitive data for the application's functionality. For example, only returning some of the digits of a credit card number and not the full number. If the complete data is required, it should be masked in the user interface unless the user specifically views it.

Verify that sensitive information is subject to data retention classification, ensuring that outdated or unnecessary data is deleted automatically, on a defined schedule, or as the situation requires.
Verify that sensitive information is removed from the metadata of user-submitted files unless storage is consented to by the user.

Verify that authenticated data is cleared from client storage, such as the browser DOM, after the client or session is terminated. The 'Clear-Site-Data' HTTP response header field may be able to help with this but the client-side should also be able to clear up if the server connection is not available when the session is terminated.
Items.Evidence: Logout clears auth cookies and deletes the server session; the web app clears its local state on logout. No Clear-Site-Data header is sent and offline cleanup is not guaranteed.

Items.Description: Verify that the application sets sufficient anti-caching HTTP response header fields (i.e., Cache-Control: no-store) so that sensitive data is not cached in browsers.
Items.Evidence: Originals are served with 'private, no-cache, no-transform' and thumbnails with 'private, max-age...' (cacheControlHeaders in server/src/utils/file.ts); responses are not marked no-store across the API.

Items.Description: Verify that data stored in browser storage (such as localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB, or cookies) does not contain sensitive data, with the exception of session tokens.
Items.Evidence: Browser storage contains only UI preferences (search query type, scroll position); session tokens live in HttpOnly cookies, and the non-HttpOnly isAuthenticated cookie only signals auth state.

Items.Description: Verify that application documentation defines risk based remediation time frames for 3rd party component versions with vulnerabilities and for updating libraries in general, to minimize the risk from these components.
Items.Evidence: No documentation defines risk-based remediation time frames for vulnerable dependencies; renovate.json automates update PRs but has no security-timeframe policy.

Items.Description: Verify that an inventory catalog, such as software bill of materials (SBOM), is maintained of all third-party libraries in use, including verifying that components come from pre-defined, trusted, and continually maintained repositories.
Items.Evidence: No SBOM is maintained in the repository; dependency tracking relies on lockfiles and GitHub's dependency graph.

Items.Description: Verify that the application documentation identifies functionality which is time-consuming or resource-demanding. This must include how to prevent a loss of availability due to overusing this functionality and how to avoid a situation where building a response takes longer than the consumer's timeout. Potential defenses may include asynchronous processing, using queues, and limiting parallel processes per user and per application.
Items.Evidence: docs describe hardware transcoding and job queues at a high level, but there is no documentation identifying resource-demanding functionality and defenses against availability loss.

Items.Description: Verify that application documentation highlights third-party libraries which are considered to be "risky components".
Verify that application documentation highlights parts of the application where "dangerous functionality" is being used.
Verify that the application only contains components which have not breached the documented update and remediation time frames.
Items.Evidence: Renovate continuously updates dependencies, but there is no policy or verification that components stay within defined remediation time frames.

Items.Description: Verify that the application has implemented defenses against loss of availability due to functionality which is time-consuming or resource-demanding, based on the documented security decisions and strategies for this.
Items.Evidence: Heavy work (thumbnailing, transcoding, ML) runs asynchronously through BullMQ job queues with per-queue concurrency limits and job deduplication; upload/download streams are throttled by backpressure. Covered partially by job service specs.

Items.Description: Verify that the production environment only includes functionality that is required for the application to function, and does not expose extraneous functionality such as test code, sample snippets, and development functionality.
Items.Evidence: Dev-only behavior is gated behind isDev() (CORS, swagger writing); the production image contains only built server/web artifacts, but the Swagger UI remains exposed in production.

Items.Description: Verify that third-party components and all of their transitive dependencies are included from the expected repository, whether internally owned or an external source, and that there is no risk of a dependency confusion attack.

Verify that the application implements additional protections around parts of the application which are documented as containing "dangerous functionality" or using third-party libraries considered to be "risky components". This could include techniques such as sandboxing, encapsulation, containerization or network level isolation to delay and deter attackers who compromise one part of an application from pivoting elsewhere in the application.

Verify that the application only returns the required subset of fields from a data object. For example, it should not return an entire data object, as some individual fields should not be accessible to users.
Items.Evidence: API responses are produced by explicit DTO mappers that whitelist fields (mapUser/mapUserAdmin never include password hashes); response shapes asserted in service and controller specs.

Items.Description: Verify that where the application backend makes calls to external URLs, it is configured to not follow redirects unless it is intended functionality.
Items.Evidence: Outbound fetches (version check, ML ping, OAuth metadata/JWKS) use default redirect-following; the URLs are fixed constants or admin-configured, which limits but does not eliminate redirect-based SSRF.

Items.Description: Verify that the application has countermeasures to protect against mass assignment attacks by limiting allowed fields per controller and action, e.g., it is not possible to insert or update a field value when it was not intended to be part of that action.
Items.Evidence: All write endpoints accept zod DTOs that strip unknown keys; entity updates map only whitelisted fields, so mass assignment of unintended fields is not possible. Covered by validation and service specs.

Items.Description: Verify that all proxying and middleware components transfer the user's original IP address correctly using trusted data fields that cannot be manipulated by the end user, and the application and web server use this correct value for logging and security decisions such as rate limiting, taking into account that even the original IP address may not be reliable due to dynamic IPs, VPNs, or corporate firewalls.
Items.Evidence: Express trust proxy is restricted to loopback + configured trustedProxies, so clientIp used for logging/security decisions comes only from trusted hops; covered by config repository specs.

Items.Description: Verify that the application explicitly ensures that variables are of the correct type and performs strict equality and comparator operations. This is to avoid type juggling or type confusion vulnerabilities caused by the application code making an assumption about a variable type.
Items.Evidence: TypeScript with strict type checking and zod runtime validation enforces correct types; comparisons use strict equality consistently (lint-enforced) preventing type juggling.

Items.Description: Verify that JavaScript code is written in a way that prevents prototype pollution, for example, by using Set() or Map() instead of object literals.
Items.Evidence: User input is parsed into fresh objects by zod (no recursive merge of user-controlled keys into prototypes); no prototype-pollution-prone deep-merge utilities were found, though there is no explicit hardening test.

Items.Description: Verify that the application has defenses against HTTP parameter pollution attacks, particularly if the application framework makes no distinction about the source of request parameters (query string, body parameters, cookies, or header fields).
Items.Evidence: Header extraction takes the first value deliberately (fromMaybeArray in utils/request.ts) and zod rejects unexpected duplicates for most inputs, but there is no systematic HTTP parameter pollution defense.

Items.Description: Verify that shared objects in multi-threaded code (such as caches, files, or in-memory objects accessed by multiple threads) are accessed safely by using thread-safe types and synchronization mechanisms like locks or semaphores to avoid race conditions and data corruption.

Verify that checks on a resource's state, such as its existence or permissions, and the actions that depend on them are performed as a single atomic operation to prevent time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) race conditions. For example, checking if a file exists before opening it, or verifying a user’s access before granting it.

Verify that locks are used consistently to avoid threads getting stuck, whether by waiting on each other or retrying endlessly, and that locking logic stays within the code responsible for managing the resource to ensure locks cannot be inadvertently or maliciously modified by external classes or code.

Verify that resource allocation policies prevent thread starvation by ensuring fair access to resources, such as by leveraging thread pools, allowing lower-priority threads to proceed within a reasonable timeframe.

Verify that an inventory exists documenting the logging performed at each layer of the application's technology stack, what events are being logged, log formats, where that logging is stored, how it is used, how access to it is controlled, and for how long logs are kept.
Items.Evidence: No logging inventory exists; logging behavior (stdout/JSON, levels, telemetry) is only implicitly defined by the code and env variables.

Items.Description: Verify that each log entry includes necessary metadata (such as when, where, who, what) that would allow for a detailed investigation of the timeline when an event happens.
Items.Evidence: Log entries include timestamp, severity, app context and a per-request correlation id via AsyncLocalStorage (logging.repository.ts, logging.interceptor.ts), but not the acting user or target resource in every entry.

Items.Description: Verify that time sources for all logging components are synchronized, and that timestamps in security event metadata use UTC or include an explicit time zone offset. UTC is recommended to ensure consistency across distributed systems and to prevent confusion during daylight saving time transitions.
Items.Evidence: Timestamps come from the host clock in ISO format; UTC usage is not enforced and time synchronization is a deployment concern.

Items.Description: Verify that the application only stores or broadcasts logs to the files and services that are documented in the log inventory.
Items.Evidence: Logs go to stdout (optionally JSON) and optionally to OTLP telemetry endpoints; destinations are bounded by env config but not by a documented inventory.

Items.Description: Verify that logs can be read and correlated by the log processor that is in use, preferably by using a common logging format.
Items.Evidence: A JSON log format is available (LogFormat json via env) and the console format is consistent, allowing correlation by log processors.

Items.Description: Verify that when logging sensitive data, the application enforces logging based on the data's protection level. For example, it may not be allowed to log certain data, such as credentials or payment details. Other data, such as session tokens, may only be logged by being hashed or masked, either in full or partially.
Items.Evidence: Passwords/tokens are not logged by the logger, but user emails are logged on failed login (auth.service.ts warn) and no formal protection-level-based logging rules or redaction pipeline exist.

Items.Description: Verify that all authentication operations are logged, including successful and unsuccessful attempts. Additional metadata, such as the type of authentication or factors used, should also be collected.
Items.Evidence: Failed logins are logged with IP and email (auth.service.ts); successful logins create session rows (device/OS/IP recorded) rather than log lines; no factor metadata is logged. Partially covered by auth service specs.

Items.Description: Verify that failed authorization attempts are logged. For L3, this must include logging all authorization decisions, including logging when sensitive data is accessed (without logging the sensitive data itself).
Items.Evidence: Failed authorization attempts (403 from AuthGuard/access checks) are not systematically logged.

Items.Description: Verify that the application logs the security events that are defined in the documentation and also logs attempts to bypass the security controls, such as input validation, business logic, and anti-automation.
Items.Evidence: Some security events are logged (failed logins, upload validation failures) but there is no defined security event list and bypass attempts (validation, anti-automation) are not logged.

Items.Description: Verify that the application logs unexpected errors and security control failures such as backend TLS failures.
Items.Evidence: Unexpected errors are caught by the global exception filter and logged with stack traces (middleware/global-exception.filter.ts); job failures are logged via the job repository.

Items.Description: Verify that all logging components appropriately encode data to prevent log injection.
Items.Evidence: Log messages are built via template literals into structured entries; user-controlled values (e.g. email in login warnings) are included without encoding, so log injection via newlines is not fully prevented.

Items.Description: Verify that logs are protected from unauthorized access and cannot be modified.
Items.Evidence: Logs are written to container stdout with normal file permissions; protection against unauthorized access/modification is a deployment (Docker/host) concern, not enforced by the app.

Items.Description: Verify that logs are securely transmitted to a logically separate system for analysis, detection, alerting, and escalation. The aim is to ensure that if the application is breached, the logs are not compromised.
Items.Evidence: Optional OTLP telemetry can ship signals to a separate collector (telemetry.repository.ts), but logs themselves are not transmitted to a separate system by default.

Items.Description: Verify that a generic message is returned to the consumer when an unexpected or security-sensitive error occurs, ensuring no exposure of sensitive internal system data such as stack traces, queries, secret keys, and tokens.
Items.Evidence: The global exception filter maps errors to generic HTTP exceptions without stack traces or SQL; unhandled errors return a generic 500 message. Covered by error interceptor/filter specs.

Items.Description: Verify that the application continues to operate securely when external resource access fails, for example, by using patterns such as circuit breakers or graceful degradation.
Items.Evidence: Failures of external resources (ML service, Redis, DB) are handled with retries/queue re-runs and logged errors rather than crashing, but there is no circuit-breaker pattern.

Items.Description: Verify that the application fails gracefully and securely, including when an exception occurs, preventing fail-open conditions such as processing a transaction despite errors resulting from validation logic.
Items.Evidence: The app fails closed: AuthGuard throws on any validation error (no fail-open), zod validation rejects malformed input, and upload errors abort the pipeline; covered by guard and validation specs.

Items.Description: Verify that a "last resort" error handler is defined which will catch all unhandled exceptions. This is both to avoid losing error details that must go to log files and to ensure that an error does not take down the entire application process, leading to a loss of availability.

Verify that the Traversal Using Relays around NAT (TURN) service only allows access to IP addresses that are not reserved for special purposes (e.g., internal networks, broadcast, loopback). Note that this applies to both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses.
Items.Evidence: No TURN service or NAT traversal exists; Immich does not use WebRTC.

Items.Description: Verify that the Traversal Using Relays around NAT (TURN) service is not susceptible to resource exhaustion when legitimate users attempt to open a large number of ports on the TURN server.
Verify that the key for the Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) certificate is managed and protected based on the documented policy for management of cryptographic keys.
Items.Evidence: No DTLS/SRTP media server exists; streaming is done via HTTP(S) progressive download and HLS/DASH from the app server.

Items.Description: Verify that the media server is configured to use and support approved Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) cipher suites and a secure protection profile for the DTLS Extension for establishing keys for the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (DTLS-SRTP).
Items.Evidence: No DTLS-SRTP media server exists in the stack.

Items.Description: Verify that Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP) authentication is checked at the media server to prevent Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) injection attacks from leading to either a Denial of Service condition or audio or video media insertion into media streams.
Items.Evidence: No SRTP streams are processed by the application.

Items.Description: Verify that the media server is able to continue processing incoming media traffic when encountering malformed Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP) packets.
Items.Evidence: No SRTP packets are handled by the application.

Items.Description: Verify that the media server is able to continue processing incoming media traffic during a flood of Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP) packets from legitimate users.

Verify that the media server is not susceptible to the "ClientHello" Race Condition vulnerability in Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) by checking if the media server is publicly known to be vulnerable or by performing the race condition test.

Verify that any audio or video recording mechanisms associated with the media server are able to continue processing incoming media traffic during a flood of Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP) packets from legitimate users.

Verify that the Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) certificate is checked against the Session Description Protocol (SDP) fingerprint attribute, terminating the media stream if the check fails, to ensure the authenticity of the media stream.

Verify that the signaling server is able to continue processing legitimate incoming signaling messages during a flood attack. This should be achieved by implementing rate limiting at the signaling level.
Items.Evidence: No WebRTC signaling server exists (socket.io is used for app notifications, not media signaling).

Items.Description: Verify that the signaling server is able to continue processing legitimate signaling messages when encountering malformed signaling message that could cause a denial of service condition. This could include implementing input validation, safely handling integer overflows, preventing buffer overflows, and employing other robust error-handling techniques.
Items.Evidence: No WebRTC signaling messages are processed by the application.
